_meta: The spans emitted by one request as it fans out across services, used to show why a distributed trace must propagate span context -- a trace id shared by all spans plus each span's own id and its parent span's id -- rather than only a flat correlation id shared by every log line. A correlation id groups all the events of one request together, which is a real improvement over an unlabeled jumble, but it is flat: it says these events belong to the same request and nothing about their structure. It cannot tell you which service called which, and it cannot tell you where the time actually went, because span durations nest. A parent span's duration already contains its children's durations -- the gateway is 'busy' for the whole request while it waits on the database, which is busy while it waits on the cache -- so summing all the durations double-counts the nested time and produces a total larger than the request's wall-clock time. Worse, the span with the largest total duration is usually a caller that is mostly waiting, not the real hotspot: the fix is to reconstruct the call tree from the parent pointers and compute each span's self-time -- its own duration minus the time inside its children -- which attributes each slice of wall-clock time to exactly one span and reveals the true bottleneck. On this fixture the gateway (100ms) contains auth (20ms) and the database (60ms), and the database contains the cache (50ms). By total duration the database looks like the bottleneck at 60ms, but its self-time is only 10ms -- it spends 50ms waiting on the cache, whose self-time of 50ms is the real hotspot. spans is the list of spans, each with span_id, parent_id (null for the root), service, start_ms, and duration_ms. It is the fixture; the flat duration sum, the reconstructed tree, the self-times, and the two bottleneck picks are computed.
